title: Smart Contract Security & Auditing
tagline: Think like an attacker: bug classes, reentrancy, oracles, tools, audit reports and incident response
summary: A hands-on introduction to smart contract security and the audit process: access control, reentrancy, arithmetic and rounding, tx.origin, weak randomness, denial of service, oracles and flash loans, signatures and upgrades, tools and manual review, writing findings and responding to incidents. Every Solidity listing was compiled against OpenZeppelin 5. You run the code in your own tools; this course does not by itself qualify you as an auditor.

modules.title: The threat landscape
modules.summary: Why contracts are different to secure, how attackers think and the bug classes behind most losses.
modules.outcome: You can explain why contract security is hard, name the main bug classes and fix a missing access check.
modules.intro: Smart contracts are public programs that hold money and cannot easily be patched. Anyone can read the code, call it in any order and fund an attack with a flash loan. This module explains the mindset and the catalogue of common bugs that the rest of the course explores in depth.

topics.title: Why contract security is different
topics.html:
A web application sits behind a server you control. You can patch it tonight, roll back, block an address and call the bank. A deployed contract is different on every count: the code is visible to everyone, it holds value directly, it is often immutable, and transactions are final. A bug can be found and exploited by anyone in the world within minutes of deployment.

Web application versus smart contract
PropertyTypical web appSmart contract
Code visibilityPrivatePublic (or easily decompiled)
Fixing a bugDeploy a patchHard or impossible without a planned upgrade path
Holds valueUsually through a bankDirectly in the contract
Attacker's toolsProbing a live serviceExact local copies, simulations and free flash loans
Undo a mistakeRefunds and rollbacksFinal: no central undo
Cost of an attackTime and effortOften one transaction
Definition

Attack surface. Every way an outsider can interact with your system: each external function, each signature check, each admin power, each token or contract you call and each price you read.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is a deployed contract bug so serious?
  • The code is public, holds value and is often hard to patch (correct)
  • The code is hidden
  • Bugs are impossible
  • Nobody can call it

Public and final.

Tip

Think like an attacker with unlimited free capital for one transaction. If that attacker can profit, assume someone will try.

Check what you just learned

1. An attacker's biggest advantage against a contract is that:
  • They know your password
  • The code is public and capital can be borrowed free for a transaction (correct)
  • Contracts are slow
  • Contracts are private

Public code and flash loans.
keyPoints: Contracts are public, hold value and are hard to patch.
The attack surface is every way outsiders can interact with them.

topics.title: Access control failures
topics.html:
The first wallet checks the owner when withdrawing, which looks careful. But setOwner has no check, so a stranger calls it, becomes the owner and withdraws. A permission check is only as strong as the weakest function that can change who has permission.

Where access control goes wrong
MistakeExampleFix
No check on a sensitive functionsetOwner, mint, pause, upgradeonlyOwner or a role check on every privileged function
Unprotected initialiserinitialize() can be called by anyone after deploymentUse initialiser guards and call it in the same transaction as deployment
Default visibility surprisesAn internal helper accidentally made public or externalBe explicit and review every public function
Single powerful keyOne externally owned account holds all admin powerMulti-signature wallet and time-lock
Role mix-upsThe pauser can also move fundsSeparate roles with least privilege

A quick test for any function

  1. What does this change?
  2. Who is allowed to call it?
  3. Where is that enforced in the code?
  4. Can that permission itself be changed, and by whom?
  5. Is there a test that calls it from a stranger's account and expects a revert?

Check what you just learned

1. What is wrong with BrokenWallet?
  • withdrawAll has a check
  • It has a constructor
  • setOwner can be called by anyone (correct)
  • It accepts ETH

Ownership can be taken.

Check what you just learned

1. The best test for access control is to:
  • Rename the owner
  • Read the comments
  • Check gas
  • Call each privileged function from a stranger and expect a revert (correct)

Test the negative case.
keyPoints: Every privileged function needs an enforced permission check.
A check is only as strong as the weakest way to change who may pass it.

topics.title: A catalogue of bug classes
topics.html:
The main classes
ClassOne-line summaryCovered in
Access controlAnyone can do what only an admin shouldThis module
ReentrancyAn external call lets an attacker re-enter before state is updatedModule 2
Arithmetic and roundingTruncation, precision loss, unsafe castsModule 3
Logic and design flawsThe code does what it says but not what was intendedModule 3
Denial of serviceOne failing recipient or a growing loop blocks everyoneModule 3
Oracle and price manipulationTrusting a price an attacker can moveModule 4
Signature and replay bugsReusing a valid signature where it should not workModule 4
Upgrade and proxy bugsStorage collisions and unprotected initialisersModule 4

Most large losses are not exotic cryptography failures. They are the same handful of mistakes: a missing check, an unsafe order of operations, a trusted price or a misunderstood assumption about someone else's contract. Knowing the catalogue lets you spot them quickly in unfamiliar code.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a well-known library makes your own code safe.
  • Believing the compiler version solves logic bugs.
  • Reviewing only the main function and ignoring helpers and admin paths.

Check what you just learned

1. Most big contract losses come from:
  • A handful of familiar mistakes (correct)
  • Broken cryptography
  • Slow blocks
  • Short names

The same classes keep recurring.

Check what you just learned

1. A good first step in a review is to:
  • Optimise gas
  • List entry points and where value moves (correct)
  • Rename functions
  • Add comments

Map the surface first.

Key terms: flip and sort

Attack surface
All the ways outsiders can interact with a system
Access control
Rules about who may call what
Initialiser
A function that sets up state after deployment
Least privilege
Giving each account only the power it needs
Multi-signature wallet
A wallet needing several approvals
Flash loan
An uncollateralised loan repaid within one transaction
keyPoints: A handful of bug classes cause most losses.
A reviewer lists entry points, value flows and external dependencies first.

modules.title: Reentrancy and state discipline
modules.summary: How reentrancy works, how to fix it in order and with guards, and the subtler cross-function forms.
modules.outcome: You can trace a reentrancy attack, apply checks-effects-interactions and explain when a guard is also needed.
modules.intro: Reentrancy is the best-known contract bug because it can drain a whole system from one small mistake. It is simple to fix once you understand it, which makes it a perfect first case study in how an attacker thinks.

topics.title: Anatomy of a reentrancy attack
topics.html:
The bug is not in the arithmetic. It is in the order: the bank hands control to an outsider before it has finished recording what it just did. While the outsider is running, the bank's books are still wrong.

Drain simulator

Change how much the attacker deposits and the number of recursive calls to see how much leaves the vault. A teaching model.

Adjust Other people's funds (ETH), Attacker deposit (ETH), Reentrant calls in one transaction and see Taken in one transaction (ETH), Transactions to empty the vault change.

Check what you just learned

1. What makes reentrancy possible in VulnerableBank?
  • Overflow
  • Missing events
  • The balance is cleared after the ETH is sent (correct)
  • A long name

Control is handed over too early.

Check what you just learned

1. During the external call, the bank's balance record for the attacker is:
  • Already zero
  • Deleted
  • Negative
  • Still the old value (correct)

That is the flaw.
keyPoints: Reentrancy exploits handing over control before state is updated.
The attacker's receive function calls back in while the books are stale.

topics.title: Fixes: order first, guard second
topics.html:
Two layers of defence
LayerHow it helpsWeakness alone
Checks-effects-interactionsState is correct before control leaves the contract, so a re-entry sees the updated balance and failsEasy to break by mistake when code is changed later
nonReentrant guardA lock that reverts any second entry into guarded functionsDoes not protect other, unguarded functions that share state
Pull paymentsMoney moves only when the recipient asks, in a function that follows the patternNeeds consistent bookkeeping

Rules of thumb

  1. Update every piece of state the function depends on before any external call.
  2. Treat every call to an unknown address as hostile, including token transfers.
  3. Use a guard on functions that move value, as a second layer.
  4. Prefer the pull-payment pattern for distributing money.
  5. Never rely on a fixed gas stipend to stop reentrancy.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use both CEI and a nonReentrant guard?
  • Each protects where the other can fail (correct)
  • They are the same thing
  • Guards cost nothing
  • CEI is deprecated

Defence in depth.

Watch out

Do not write clever reentrancy defences of your own. Use the well-reviewed order of operations and an audited guard.

Check what you just learned

1. Checks-effects-interactions means:
  • Interact, then check
  • Validate, update state, then call out (correct)
  • Update nothing
  • Call out first

The order of work.
keyPoints: Update state before external calls: checks, effects, interactions.
Add a guard as a second layer and prefer pull payments.

topics.title: Subtler forms: cross-function and read-only
topics.html:
Beyond the simple case
FormHow it worksDefence
Cross-function reentrancyDuring a call from function A, the attacker calls function B that shares the same stale stateApply the guard or the order to every function touching that state
Cross-contract reentrancyTwo contracts of the same system share assumptions; one is re-entered through the otherTreat the whole system's state as one unit and order updates accordingly
Read-only reentrancyDuring an external call, another contract reads a view function whose values are temporarily wrongGuard view functions that other protocols rely on, or update state before calls
Token hook reentrancyToken standards with callbacks call your contract during transfersAssume any token call may call back

These variants share one root cause: somewhere, a value is read while the system is in the middle of changing it. The cure is also the same: finish changing the system's state before anyone else is given control, and keep the number of places where state can be seen mid-update as small as possible.

Common mistakes

  • Guarding one function but not another that reads or changes the same variable.
  • Updating a balance but not the total that other code relies on, before calling out.
  • Assuming ERC-20 transfers can never call back.

Check what you just learned

1. Read-only reentrancy happens when:
  • Gas is low
  • Nothing is read
  • A view function is read mid-update by another contract (correct)
  • An event is missing

Temporarily wrong values are observed.

Check what you just learned

1. Cross-function reentrancy means the attacker calls:
  • The same function only
  • A library
  • Nothing
  • A different function that shares stale state (correct)

Shared state is the target.

Key terms: flip and sort

Reentrancy
Calling back into a contract before it has finished
Checks-effects-interactions
Validate, update state, then call out
nonReentrant
A modifier that blocks nested entry
Pull payment
Recipients withdraw their own funds
Cross-function reentrancy
Re-entry through a different function
Callback
An external call that returns control to you
keyPoints: Reentrancy can cross functions and contracts.
Finish all state updates before handing over control.

modules.title: Arithmetic, logic and design flaws
modules.summary: Rounding and precision, unsafe casts, tx.origin, weak randomness, denial of service and front-running.
modules.outcome: You can spot rounding and precision bugs, avoid tx.origin and weak randomness, and design out denial of service.
modules.intro: Not all bugs are exotic. Many come from arithmetic that looks fine, from using the wrong piece of blockchain data, or from designs that let one participant block the rest. This module covers the most common ones.

topics.title: Rounding, precision and casts
topics.html:
Solidity has no decimals. Division drops the remainder, so 5 / 2 is 2. That is predictable, but it matters when the number is money or shares. If a user deposits 1,500 into a vault with 1,000,000 of assets and 1,000 shares, the shares they receive are 1500 × 1000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 1.5, which rounds down to 1. That one share is worth 1,000, so the depositor silently loses 500.

Rules for safe division
RuleWhy
Multiply before dividingDividing first throws away precision that multiplication cannot recover
Round in the protocol's favourDown for what you pay out, up for what you must receive
Use fixed-point scaling (for example 1e18)Keeps fractions as whole numbers
Guard against division by zeroAn empty pool or vault has no valid price
Avoid casting to smaller types without checksuint8(x) silently truncates in older code; use safe casting libraries
Think about tiny and huge valuesRounding bugs live at the extremes

Check what you just learned

1. Why multiply before dividing?
  • It keeps precision that division would discard (correct)
  • It is cheaper
  • It is required by the compiler
  • It avoids events

Do divisions last.

Tip

Write down for every division which party benefits from the rounding. If you cannot answer, you do not understand the bug risk yet.

Check what you just learned

1. 5 / 2 in Solidity equals:
  • 2.5
  • 2 (correct)
  • 3
  • 1

The remainder is dropped.
keyPoints: Integer division drops the remainder; multiply first and round to protect the protocol.
Scale fractions and check the extremes.

topics.title: tx.origin, randomness and timestamps
topics.html:
Why tx.origin is dangerous
FactConsequence
tx.origin is the account that began the transactionIt stays the same through a chain of contract calls
The owner calls a harmless-looking malicious contractThat contract calls the wallet; tx.origin is still the owner
The wallet checks tx.origin == ownerThe check passes and funds move to the thief
Use msg.sender insteadIt is the direct caller, so the malicious contract is rejected

Values such as block.timestamp, block.prevrandao and the player count are visible to everyone and can be influenced by the block producer or predicted by another contract. A lottery that uses them can be gamed. Real randomness needs a verifiable random function (VRF) from an oracle network, or a commit-and-reveal scheme in which participants first commit a hidden value and later reveal it.

Rules

  • Never use tx.origin for authorisation.
  • Never use block values as a source of randomness for anything valuable.
  • Treat timestamps as accurate to a few seconds at best.
  • Use a verifiable random function for fair draws.

Check what you just learned

1. Why does the phishing attack work?
  • The wallet checks msg.sender
  • The owner has no keys
  • tx.origin is still the owner even though a malicious contract made the call (correct)
  • Gas is low

tx.origin does not change along the chain.

Check what you just learned

1. A safe source of randomness for a valuable lottery is:
  • block.timestamp
  • The gas price
  • The player count
  • A verifiable random function (correct)

Block data can be predicted or nudged.
keyPoints: Authorise with msg.sender, never tx.origin.
Block data is not random: use a verifiable random function.

topics.title: Denial of service and front-running
topics.html:
Denial-of-service patterns
PatternHow it blocksFix
Push payments in a loopOne recipient that reverts stops the whole loopPull payments: record what is owed and let users claim
Unbounded loopsThe array grows until the loop cannot fit in one blockBound the work or process in batches
Dependence on a call succeedingAn external contract is paused or removedHandle failure gracefully or isolate it
Forced ETHSomeone sends ETH to break a strict balance checkDo not assume the balance equals your own accounting

Front-running is different: transactions wait in a public pool before they are included, so anyone can see them and pay a higher fee to go first. A bot that sees your large purchase can buy before you and sell after you. Defences include slippage limits, commit-and-reveal designs, private submission services and designs where the order of transactions matters less.

Check what you just learned

1. Why are pull payments safer?
  • One failing recipient cannot block the rest (correct)
  • They use less gas always
  • They need no state
  • They are private

Isolation of failure.

Watch out

A pull-payment design shifts the responsibility to the recipient. Make sure the bookkeeping is right before any claim is paid.

Check what you just learned

1. Front-running is possible because:
  • Blocks are private
  • Pending transactions are public (correct)
  • Gas is free
  • Contracts are slow

Anyone can see and react.

Key terms: flip and sort

Precision loss
Information lost when integer division drops remainders
tx.origin
The account that started the transaction
VRF
A verifiable random function
Commit-and-reveal
Hide a value, then show it later
Denial of service
Blocking others from using a contract
Front-running
Acting first on a visible pending transaction
keyPoints: Avoid loops that depend on every external call succeeding.
Transactions are public before inclusion, so design with front-running in mind.

modules.title: Oracles, flash loans and external dependencies
modules.summary: Price manipulation, oracle checks, flash loans, delegatecall risks, signature replay and upgrade bugs.
modules.outcome: You can explain a flash-loan price attack, apply oracle sanity checks and name the risks of delegatecall, replay and upgrades.
modules.intro: Contracts rarely stand alone: they read prices, call tokens, accept signatures and sit behind proxies. Each dependency is a place where an assumption can fail. Many of the largest losses came from trusting something an attacker could change.

topics.title: Price manipulation and oracles
topics.html:
Oracle design checks
CheckWhy
Use an independent, manipulation-resistant sourceA single pool's spot price can be moved
Prefer time-weighted averages for on-chain pricesA single transaction cannot move an average over many blocks
Reject zero or negative pricesA broken feed can return nonsense
Reject stale pricesOld data may not reflect the market
Sanity-check against a bound or a second sourceDetect large unexplained jumps
Plan for feed failurePause or fall back safely

Check what you just learned

1. Why is a single pool's spot price a bad oracle?
  • It is slow
  • It is too accurate
  • A flash loan can move it within one transaction (correct)
  • It is private

Manipulable.

Check what you just learned

1. A flash loan must be:
  • Secured by a house
  • Repaid next year
  • Never repaid
  • Repaid in the same transaction (correct)

Otherwise the transaction reverts.
keyPoints: Spot prices can be moved in one transaction using flash loans.
Use robust oracles and check freshness and validity.

topics.title: Delegatecall, signatures and untrusted tokens
topics.html:
Three more trust boundaries
BoundaryRiskDefence
delegatecall to a user-supplied addressThe target's code runs on your storage and can rewrite the ownerOnly delegatecall to fixed, trusted implementations
Off-chain signaturesA valid signature reused on another chain, contract or timeInclude chain id, contract address, nonce and expiry; use EIP-712
Arbitrary tokensFee-on-transfer tokens deliver less than requested; hooks call back; some tokens do not return valuesMeasure the balance change; use safe transfer wrappers; guard against callbacks
Low-level call resultsA call can fail silently if you ignore the returned booleanAlways check success
Self-destruct and forced ETHBalance changes without your code runningDo not rely on address(this).balance for accounting

The thread through all of these is that you must not assume anything about code you did not write. If a token behaves strangely, if a signature is replayed, if a delegate target is hostile, your contract's guarantees only hold if you designed for it.

Defensive habits

  1. Make a list of every external contract your code calls and what you assume about each.
  2. Check every returned value.
  3. Compute balances by what you recorded, not what you observe.
  4. Include domain data in everything that is signed.
  5. Prefer well-audited wrappers to hand-written low-level code.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is delegatecall to a user-supplied address dangerous?
  • The target's code runs against your storage and can change anything (correct)
  • It costs gas
  • It emits no events
  • It is deprecated

Your storage becomes theirs to edit.

Check what you just learned

1. A fee-on-transfer token means:
  • You receive more
  • You receive less than the amount sent (correct)
  • Nothing changes
  • It is free

Measure the balance change.
keyPoints: Every external dependency is an assumption that can fail.
Bind signatures, check results and never delegatecall to unknown code.

topics.title: Upgrade and proxy risks
topics.html:
Where upgradeable systems fail
FailureHow it happensDefence
Unprotected initialiserAnyone calls initialize on the proxy or implementation and becomes ownerInitialiser guards, disabling initialisers in the implementation, and initialising in the deployment transaction
Storage collisionA new version changes the order or type of variablesAppend-only layouts, storage gaps, layout checks in tests
Upgrade by a single keyA stolen key replaces the logic with a malicious oneMulti-signature wallet and time-lock, with public notice
Self-destruct in an implementationA destroyed implementation breaks every proxy using itAvoid self-destruct; protect and disable the implementation
Missing upgrade function in a UUPS versionThe system can never be upgraded againTests that run an upgrade of the upgrade

Upgradeability trades immutability for flexibility. Users must trust whoever can upgrade. For many systems the right answer is a clear, limited upgrade path with delay and public visibility; for others it is no upgrade path at all. Whichever you choose, say so openly.

Watch out

An upgrade is a new deployment of your risk. Every upgrade deserves its own review, rehearsal and announcement.

Check what you just learned

1. Why do upgrade keys deserve a time-lock?
  • To save gas
  • To hide upgrades
  • To give users time to react before logic changes (correct)
  • To rename contracts

Transparency and exit.

Check what you just learned

1. An unprotected initialiser lets:
  • Events vanish
  • Nobody act
  • Gas fall
  • Anyone become the owner (correct)

Set-up functions are privileged.

Key terms: flip and sort

Oracle
A source of outside data for a contract
Spot price
The current price in a single pool
TWAP
A time-weighted average price
Flash loan
A loan borrowed and repaid in one transaction
Stale data
Old data that no longer reflects reality
Fee-on-transfer token
A token that takes a cut when moved
keyPoints: Initialisers, storage layout and upgrade keys are the main risks.
Use time-locks, multi-signature control and rehearsals.

modules.title: Tools and methodology
modules.summary: Static analysis, fuzzing and invariants, manual review, threat modelling and defence in depth.
modules.outcome: You can combine tools and human review into a repeatable process and defend a design in depth.
modules.intro: No single technique finds everything. Professionals combine fast automated tools, deep randomised testing and careful human reading, and they build their designs so that one failure is not fatal.

topics.title: Automated tools and their limits
topics.html:
What each technique is good for
TechniqueGood atWeak at
Static analysis (for example Slither)Known patterns, bad practice, quick feedbackBusiness logic and novel bugs; false positives
FuzzingEdge cases, arithmetic and unexpected inputsNeeds good properties to check
Invariant testingAccounting and state rules across call sequencesQuality depends on how the handlers are written
Symbolic executionExploring paths to find assertion failuresSlow on large systems
Formal verificationProving chosen properties for all inputsSpecialist skill; only covers what you specify
Manual reviewIntent, design and logic flawsSlow, depends on the reviewer

Run static analysis on every commit: it is cheap and catches careless mistakes. Treat its output as hints to investigate, not a verdict. A clean report does not mean a safe contract, and a long report does not mean a broken one.

Make tools part of the routine

  • Run the compiler with warnings treated seriously.
  • Run static analysis in continuous integration.
  • Write fuzz and invariant tests for money and state.
  • Track coverage and look hard at untested branches.
  • Triage every finding: fix, explain or accept in writing.

Check what you just learned

1. A clean static-analysis report means:
  • No known patterns were found, but logic bugs may remain (correct)
  • The contract is safe
  • It is audited
  • Gas is low

Tools find patterns, not intent.

Check what you just learned

1. Static analysis is best at finding:
  • Business-logic flaws
  • Known bad patterns quickly (correct)
  • Intent
  • Market risk

Pattern-based.
keyPoints: Combine static analysis, fuzzing, invariants and review.
Treat tool output as hints, not a verdict.

topics.title: Manual review: how auditors read code
topics.html:
Questions for every function
QuestionLooks for
Who can call this?Missing access control
What state does it read and change?Wrong order and stale reads
What can the caller control?Unsafe inputs and arithmetic
What does it call?Reentrancy and trust assumptions
What if it is called twice, or never?Replay and stuck states
What happens at zero, one and maximum?Edge cases
Tip

Read the code the way an attacker would: not 'does this work?' but 'how could I make this do something nobody intended?'

Check what you just learned

1. Why is understanding the specification the first step?
  • It is easy
  • Auditors dislike code
  • You cannot find logic bugs without knowing the intended behaviour (correct)
  • It saves gas

Bugs are differences from intent.

Check what you just learned

1. A logic bug is found by comparing code to:
  • Its name
  • Its gas cost
  • Its length
  • Its intended behaviour (correct)

Specification versus code.
keyPoints: Auditors understand intent first, then question every function.
Ask who, what, when and what if for each entry point.

topics.title: Defence in depth
topics.html:
Layers in GuardedVault
LayerWhere
Input validationZeroAmount, Insufficient
Deposit captotalDeposits plus msg.value must not exceed the cap
Order of operationsBalances change before the external call
Reentrancy guardnonReentrant on withdraw
Emergency brakePausable stops new deposits
EventsDeposits and withdrawals are logged for monitoring
Limited admin powerThe owner can pause, but cannot move users' funds

Notice that the owner can pause new deposits but cannot withdraw anyone's money, and withdrawals are never blocked by the pause. A safety feature that also lets a compromised key steal funds is not a safety feature. Design emergency powers to stop damage, not to create new ways to cause it.

Check what you just learned

1. Why should the pause not block withdrawals in GuardedVault?
  • Users must always be able to get their money out (correct)
  • It saves gas
  • Withdrawals are free
  • It hides state

A pause should limit damage, not trap users.

Watch out

Layers help, but each new feature is also new attack surface. Keep the design as small as the job allows.

Check what you just learned

1. A deposit cap limits:
  • Gas
  • The harm from an undiscovered bug (correct)
  • Events
  • Names

A smaller prize and a smaller loss.

Key terms: flip and sort

Static analysis
Automated scanning of code for patterns
Fuzzing
Testing with many random inputs
Invariant
A property that must always hold
Formal verification
Mathematical proof of properties
Defence in depth
Several independent layers of protection
Triage
Sorting findings by importance
keyPoints: Layer validation, ordering, guards, caps and monitoring.
Emergency powers should stop damage, not create new risks.

modules.title: Audit practice and careers
modules.summary: How audits run, how to write findings, severity ranking, bug bounties and incident response.
modules.outcome: You can write a clear finding, rank severity, prepare for an audit and describe incident response honestly.
modules.intro: Finding a bug is half the job; explaining it so that someone can fix it is the other half. This module covers the audit process, the language of findings, bug bounties and what to do when something goes wrong.

topics.title: How an audit runs
topics.html:
What clients can do to get more from an audit
ActionBenefit
Freeze the code before the audit startsReviewers examine what will be deployed
Provide a clear specification and diagramsReviewers find logic flaws, not just style issues
Pass all tests and run static analysis firstTime goes to hard problems
List assumptions and areas of doubtReviewers focus where help is needed
Leave time to fix and re-checkFindings are verified, not just marked fixed

An audit is a snapshot: it examines one version of the code for a limited time. It reduces risk but cannot remove it. Any change after the audit needs fresh review, and a clean report never means 'bug-free'.

Check what you just learned

1. Why freeze the code before an audit?
  • It saves paper
  • Auditors prefer it
  • Reviewers must examine exactly what will be deployed (correct)
  • It lowers gas

A moving target cannot be reviewed.

Check what you just learned

1. An audit report means the code is:
  • Bug-free
  • Immutable
  • Insured
  • Reviewed at one version for a limited time (correct)

It reduces risk.
keyPoints: Audits are scoped, time-boxed snapshots of one code version.
Preparation and re-checking make audits more valuable.

topics.title: Writing findings and ranking severity
topics.html:
Anatomy of a finding
PartPurpose
TitleShort and specific: 'Reentrancy in withdraw'
SeverityHow serious: High, Medium, Low or informational
DescriptionWhat is wrong, where, and why
ImpactWhat an attacker can achieve in plain terms
Proof of conceptA test or steps showing it is real
RecommendationA concrete fix
StatusOpen, fixed, acknowledged or disputed
A simple severity matrix
Low likelihoodMedium likelihoodHigh likelihood
High impactMediumHighHigh
Medium impactLowMediumHigh
Low impactLowLowMedium

Writing tips

  • Lead with the impact so a busy reader sees why it matters.
  • Show, do not just claim: include a proof of concept.
  • Give a fix, not just a problem.
  • Be precise about conditions: who, when and how much.
  • Be fair: say what is good as well as what is wrong.

Check what you just learned

1. Why include a proof of concept?
  • It shows the bug is real and reproducible (correct)
  • To lengthen the report
  • It is required by law
  • It hides the bug

Evidence beats assertion.

Check what you just learned

1. High impact and low likelihood is usually:
  • Informational
  • Medium (correct)
  • Nothing
  • Critical always

Per the matrix.
keyPoints: A finding has a title, severity, description, impact, proof and fix.
Severity combines impact and likelihood.

topics.title: Bounties, incidents and honest limits
topics.html:
Bug bounties
ElementGood practice
ScopeSay exactly what is in and out of scope
RewardsScale with severity and with the funds at risk
Safe harbourPromise not to pursue good-faith researchers
ContactA clear, monitored way to report privately
ResponseAcknowledge fast, fix, then pay and thank

When an incident happens

  1. Pause what you can to stop the loss.
  2. Tell users what you know and what you do not know, quickly and honestly.
  3. Preserve evidence: transactions, logs and code versions.
  4. Involve security experts and, where it is appropriate, law enforcement.
  5. Fix, test and rehearse before redeploying.
  6. Publish a post-mortem that explains what happened and what will change.

Bounty versus loss

Change the funds at risk and the size of the bounty to see why a generous reward is often the cheapest security. A teaching model.

Adjust Funds at risk (rupees), Bounty (% of funds at risk) and see Bounty paid (rupees), Saved if the bug is reported rather than exploited (rupees) change.

Watch out

This course teaches concepts and good practice. It does not by itself qualify anyone as an auditor, and it does not make any contract safe. Real value needs experienced independent reviewers.

Check what you just learned

1. Why offer a bounty?
  • To avoid fixing bugs
  • To lower gas
  • Researchers are rewarded for reporting rather than exploiting (correct)
  • To hide code

Good incentives.

Check what you just learned

1. After an incident you should publish:
  • A discount
  • Nothing
  • A new token
  • A post-mortem (correct)

Transparency builds trust.

Key terms: flip and sort

Audit
An independent security review
Finding
A reported issue with severity and fix
Proof of concept
A demonstration that a bug is real
Severity
How serious an issue is
Bug bounty
A reward for responsibly reported bugs
Post-mortem
A written account of an incident
keyPoints: Bounties give researchers a reason to report instead of exploit.
In an incident: pause, communicate honestly, preserve evidence, fix and publish a post-mortem.
